paragraphs.text: A [ripe pu’er](shou:definition) tuo from Menghai leaf, made in 1980. Its leaf was fermented in a [wet pile](shou:wet-piling) before pressing. The pile was developed to give in weeks what raw pu’er gained only after years of keeping. The year puts this tea in the style’s first decade. In 1973 a team from the Kunming, Menghai and Xiaguan factories went to Guangzhou to [learn its piling](shou:piling-1973), and by 1975 Menghai’s method had settled into the ripe pu’er made today, five years before this tuo.

At forty-six years it is long past the decade after which the trade counts a tea as [aged ripe pu’er](shou:age-aged). The leaf goes on changing slowly with the air and moisture around it, so the way it has been kept matters as much as the years.

brewing.text: From a cake, brick or tuo, ease a piece off along the edge with a pick rather than snapping it. Whole leaves give up their flavour steadily; broken ones release it all at once and cloud the cup. Ripe pu’er takes boiling water: fermented, tightly packed leaf needs full heat to open, and it does not scald the way green tea can. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and one quick rinse, which wakes the leaf and carries off dust and any pile smell. Then short steeps that lengthen as the leaf opens, so the cup stays clear rather than heavy; it gives eight or more good cups.

notice.text: A smooth, deep cup with woody, date-like or medicinal notes, which the trade calls aged aroma.
